dus0: How to Get Up After a Fall: A Step-by-Step Guide | İhsan Eren
dus1: What should you do if you fall? What to do while waiting for help if you are hurt or cannot get up, and how to get up safely in 8 steps if you are not injured. An illustrated, step-by-step guide.
dus3: The first thing to do after a fall is not to rush. If you are not hurt and feel ready, there is a safe way to get up; if you are hurt or cannot get up, there are things you can do until help arrives. This guide takes you through the steps recommended by the NHS one at a time, with questions and pictures. Reading it once before you ever fall makes it easier to know what to do when you need to.
dus5: Stay calm and check whether you have hurt yourself
dus7: The steps to getting up safely on your own
dus8: If you have hurt your head, neck, back or hip, or cannot get up
dus9: Cover yourself and keep moving while you wait for help
dus12: Don’t rush. Stay where you are for a few minutes, steady your breathing and check whether anything hurts.
dus13: Could you have hurt your head, neck, back or hip, or do you think you won’t be able to get up?
dus15: No, I think I can get up
dus17: Call for help and keep warm
dus18: Call for help: If someone else is at home, shout to them. If your phone or personal alarm is within reach, use it; if not, bang on the wall, floor or radiator to attract attention.
dus19: Call 112: If you may have hurt your head, neck, back or hip, or you cannot get up.
dus20: Keep warm: Cover yourself with a blanket, towel or dressing gown, and put a pillow under your head. If you are on a hard floor, move onto a carpet if you can, and get out of any draught.
dus21: Keep moving: As far as you can, roll from side to side and move your arms and legs.
dus22: Have a drink: If there is a drink within reach, take sips.
dus23: If you need the toilet: Go if you need to, then roll away from the damp area.
dus27: Don’t rush. When you feel ready, roll onto your side.
dus29: Get onto your hands and knees
dus30: Push up with your arms onto your hands and knees.
dus32: Crawl to a sturdy piece of furniture
dus33: If one is not close by, crawl to a sturdy chair, sofa, bed or the bottom step of the stairs. If you get tired, stop and rest.
dus35: Put your hands on the furniture
dus36: Put both hands on the seat of the furniture or on the step and take support from it.
dus39: Bend the knee of your stronger leg, bring it forward and put that foot flat on the floor.
dus42: Lean forwards and push up slowly through your arms and legs until you are standing; bring your other foot alongside.
dus45: Holding on to the furniture, turn slowly and sit down.
dus48: Sit and rest for a while. Then tell someone that you have fallen and how you feel.
dus52: Rest for a while and tell your doctor that you fell
dus53: Even if you feel fine, a falls assessment helps you prevent further falls. You can check your risk of falling now with the 12-question fall risk check.
dus57: If you live alone, keep your phone or personal alarm with you.
dus58: Practise these steps while you are well, with someone beside you and ideally with a physiotherapist.
dus59: Keeping up your leg strength and balance both helps prevent falls and makes getting up from the floor easier.

dus63: Is it right to call 112 after a fall?
dus64: Yes. Call 112 if you think you may have hurt your head, neck, back or hip, or you cannot get up. It is fine to ask for help after a fall.
dus65: Why shouldn’t I get up straight away?
dus66: Rushing to get up while still shaken by the fall could make you fall again or make an injury worse. First stay calm, stay where you are for a few minutes, check whether anything hurts and think about whether you can get up.
dus67: Why should I keep moving if I can’t get up?
dus68: Rolling from side to side and moving your arms and legs keeps you warm, supports your circulation, and reduces stiffness and the risk of pressure sores from staying in one position for a long time.
dus69: I got up and I’m fine. Should I still see a doctor?
dus70: Yes, tell your doctor that you fell. A falls assessment may include balance tests, a review of your medicines, an eye test, a heart tracing (ECG) and blood pressure checks lying down and standing up. A home visit to spot hazards and strength and balance exercises may also be recommended.
